questions.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/1d0733f2c724253c804c596e1d0a1432b8281afa7a14a9dc6702b099ab4795e0.svg) find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m \times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n \times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,{4}^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/fdc735895573e0d7c1eb7865233dd7b56a38aeeb9c76bba77fa669212262791d.svg)
Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r ^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V_r \, \Sigma_r^+ \, U_r^T,
$$

where $\Sigma_r^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma_r.$

First, notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/d750c1c5030e0d1df7e8b14790e3f189e69346ca392d3d2885ad49db0e66b7e0.svg)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}12 & 16 & 0 \\ 9 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Reduced Singular Value Decomposition

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
The invertible matrix theorem tells us that if $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with full rank (i.e., $\mathrm{rank}(A)=n$), then there exists a unique inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ such that 

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}\!A=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

There are two questions that we can ask:

- Can we extend the notion of an inverse matrix to one that works for $n\times n$ matrices $A$ where $\mathrm{rank}(A) < n?$

- Is it possible to generalize the concept of an inverse to non-square matrices?

The answer to both questions is yes! This generalization of the inverse of $A$ is called the **pseudoinverse** of $A,$ and is denoted $A^+.$ The dimensions of $A^+$ are the same as $A^T.$

As an example, let's consider the ${\color{red}{3}}\times {\color{blue}{2}}$ matrix $A$ and its corresponding pseudoinverse, given below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/87581a69d3d76dbf3b0ebca8941c9a82b5b9443b00e86f32e4e9e4a42ef5e18b.svg)

- Computing $A^{+}\!A,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+}\,A & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which is the identity matrix $I_{\color{blue}{2}}.$

- Computing $A\!A^{+},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{+} & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which is *almost* the identity matrix $I_{\color{red}{3}}.$

We can explain this result using the following properties of the pseudoinverse:

- *If the columns of an $m\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $A^+A = I_{\color{blue}{n}}.$*

- *If the rows of an ${\color{red}{m}}\times n$ matrix $A$ are linearly independent, then $AA^+ = I_{\color{red}{m}}.$*

In the example above, the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, but the rows are not.

Moreover, the notion of a pseudoinverse is consistent with inverse matrices. In particular,

*If $A$ is an invertible square matrix, then $A^{+} = A^{-1}.$*

This lesson will discuss how to compute the pseudoinverse for any matrix, starting with an important special case.

tutorials.name: The Pseudoinverse of an Almost Diagonal Matrix
tutorials.problem:
For an *almost* zero ${\color{red}{m}}\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal only, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the *almost* zero ${\color{blue}{n}}\times {\color{red}{m}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal only.

For example, for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/d6d6a167747f99c5a48be59ae3e11ca7b5a9188e80ddeb63b8c0f193d991b18c.svg)

we calculate its pseudoinverse as follows:

- **Step 1:** Replace the non-zero elements on the main diagonal with their multiplicative inverses.

- **Step 2:** Transpose the resulting matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: The Pseudoinverse of an Almost Diagonal Matrix
tutorials.content:
For an *almost* zero ${\color{red}{m}}\times {\color{blue}{n}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
\sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r
$$

on the main diagonal only, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the *almost* zero ${\color{blue}{n}}\times {\color{red}{m}}$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}}
$$

on the main diagonal only.

For example, for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/d6d6a167747f99c5a48be59ae3e11ca7b5a9188e80ddeb63b8c0f193d991b18c.svg)

we calculate its pseudoinverse as follows:

- **Step 1:** Replace the non-zero elements on the main diagonal with their multiplicative inverses.

- **Step 2:** Transpose the resulting matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {4}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Finding the Pseudoinverse Using Singular Value Decomposition
tutorials.problem:
There are many ways to find the pseudoinverse of a given matrix $A.$ One way is to use the singular value decomposition of $A{:}$

Specifically, if 

$$
A=U \Sigma V ^T
$$

is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
A^+ = V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

 
where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$
tutorials.title: Finding the Pseudoinverse Using Singular Value Decomposition
tutorials.content:
There are many ways to find the pseudoinverse of a given matrix $A.$ One way is to use the singular value decomposition of $A{:}$

Specifically, if 

$$
A=U \Sigma V ^T
$$

is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
A^+ = V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T,
$$

 
where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$

tutorials.name: Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
tutorials.problem:
Consider the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/987aa533ca51a9f101ba590b7ade0753983ae219534342aad42054316b2e02ec.svg)

and its singular value decomposition $A=U \Sigma V ^T,$ where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/69e68ac94c6e25b2609f7d20616d7d564a1225abad748c3e4fd94516cb6df72f.svg)

Notice that $\Sigma$ contains a row of zeros. In these situations, it's possible to simplify the decomposition of $A.$ This simplified decomposition is called the **reduced singular value decomposition** of $A.$

First, we note that $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. In addition, the matrix $\Sigma$ has two non-zero singular values on its main diagonal, so the rank of $A$ is $\color{blue}r=2.$ 

To find our reduced SVD, we proceed as follows:

- First, we remove all zero rows and columns from $\Sigma.$ In our example, we should delete the $3$rd row since it contains only zeros. Notice that we obtain a square invertible matrix of rank ${\color{blue}2}{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/a56440b8808003f25bec4b61d4d06af7274a5eea68da4e94af9e91af8d64d02a.svg)

- Next, we remove all extra columns of $U$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should delete the $3$rd column:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/e4ba93ef3588affc421af821cb9de1051749396c69a9e64523399f7fc4e3bc5b.svg)

- Finally, we remove all extra columns of $V$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should keep $V$ as it is since it already has only $2$ columns: 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/b146b37075dda593ded5b86d58e6cfba3de463e01727b39756a6b90cbb88a95f.svg)

The reduced singular value decomposition of $A$ is then given by

$$
A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T.
$$

So, in our example, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/c1eed35f9b7aa3214e9783f8f80952e57adca6c4d4b81efaeb49255b5973f3af.svg)

In general, a singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T
$$

 

of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is not unique. However, we can always simplify it to the corresponding reduced singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T
$$

 

with the following properties:

- $\Sigma_r$ is a square diagonal matrix of size $r\times r,$ where $r\leq \min\{m,n\}$ is the rank of $A.$ The main diagonal of $\Sigma_r$ contains the non-zero singular values $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_r$ of $A$ in descending order.

- $U_r$ is a $m\times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $U.$

- $V_r$ is a $n \times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $V.$

tutorials.title: Reduced Singular Value Decomposition
tutorials.content:
Consider the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/987aa533ca51a9f101ba590b7ade0753983ae219534342aad42054316b2e02ec.svg)

and its singular value decomposition $A=U \Sigma V ^T,$ where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/69e68ac94c6e25b2609f7d20616d7d564a1225abad748c3e4fd94516cb6df72f.svg)

Notice that $\Sigma$ contains a row of zeros. In these situations, it's possible to simplify the decomposition of $A.$ This simplified decomposition is called the **reduced singular value decomposition** of $A.$

First, we note that $A$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix. In addition, the matrix $\Sigma$ has two non-zero singular values on its main diagonal, so the rank of $A$ is $\color{blue}r=2.$ 

To find our reduced SVD, we proceed as follows:

- First, we remove all zero rows and columns from $\Sigma.$ In our example, we should delete the $3$rd row since it contains only zeros. Notice that we obtain a square invertible matrix of rank ${\color{blue}2}{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/a56440b8808003f25bec4b61d4d06af7274a5eea68da4e94af9e91af8d64d02a.svg)

- Next, we remove all extra columns of $U$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should delete the $3$rd column:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/e4ba93ef3588affc421af821cb9de1051749396c69a9e64523399f7fc4e3bc5b.svg)

- Finally, we remove all extra columns of $V$ starting from the right, keeping only $\color{blue}2$ columns. In our example, we should keep $V$ as it is since it already has only $2$ columns: 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/b146b37075dda593ded5b86d58e6cfba3de463e01727b39756a6b90cbb88a95f.svg)

The reduced singular value decomposition of $A$ is then given by

$$
A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T.
$$

So, in our example, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14209192/assets/c1eed35f9b7aa3214e9783f8f80952e57adca6c4d4b81efaeb49255b5973f3af.svg)

In general, a singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T
$$

 

of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is not unique. However, we can always simplify it to the corresponding reduced singular value decomposition 

$$
A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T
$$

 

with the following properties:

- $\Sigma_r$ is a square diagonal matrix of size $r\times r,$ where $r\leq \min\{m,n\}$ is the rank of $A.$ The main diagonal of $\Sigma_r$ contains the non-zero singular values $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_r$ of $A$ in descending order.

- $U_r$ is a $m\times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $U.$

- $V_r$ is a $n \times r$ matrix obtained by keeping only the first $r$ columns of $V.$

tutorials.name: The Optimal Least-Squares Solution
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the least-squares solution of the system 

$$
A\mathbf x=\mathbf{b},
$$

is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that $\| A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|$ is minimized. 

The least-squares solution is not unique when $A$ has linearly dependent columns. However, it can be shown that a so-called **optimal least-squares solution** $\mathbf{x^\ast}$ always exists. The optimal least-squares solution is the solution to the least squares problem with the shortest possible length.

It turns out that the optimal least-squares solution can be found using the pseudoinverse of $A,$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf{x^\ast} = A^{+} \mathbf{b}
$$
